What makes mushrooms so amazing?

Mushrooms, which pop up all over the forest after the rain, are amazing living things that are neither plants nor animals. The secrets hidden under their caps are truly fascinating.

We've gathered all sorts of stories about mushrooms here, including mushroom facts, mushroom ecology, and fungi.

content.alt: Mushroom - Nature and science facts about mushrooms
content.text:
Nature and science facts about mushrooms

Mushrooms belong to the fungi kingdom (the mold family), so they don't photosynthesize and they don't swallow their food. Instead, they release digestive enzymes to break down organic matter and then absorb the nutrients. A mushroom is made up of a cap, gills, and a stalk, along with an underground network called mycelium. Their most important job is being a "decomposer" that breaks down dead trees and fallen leaves in the forest. Even experts find it hard to tell poisonous mushrooms apart, so you should never touch or eat wild mushrooms.

content.text:
Great points to explore together

Point out things like the cap, gills, and stalk; the mycelium (underground); their role as decomposers; and their many colors and shapes. Talking together about "What do mushrooms eat to grow?" is a wonderful way to explore (and remember, never touch wild mushrooms).

content.text:
Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Use shiitake or oyster mushrooms from the grocery store to safely observe the cap, gills, and stalk. Be sure to teach that "wild mushrooms are for looking only!" and it's great to observe mushrooms growing on dead trees in the forest from a distance.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Is a mushroom a plant?
A. No. A mushroom is a fungus (part of the mold family). It doesn't photosynthesize; it gets its nutrients by breaking down organic matter.

Q. What role do mushrooms play in the forest?
A. They're "decomposers" that break down dead trees and fallen leaves and recycle nutrients. They're essential to the forest.

Q. Is it okay to observe wild mushrooms?
A. Only look at them. Even experts find it hard to identify poisonous mushrooms, so you must never touch or eat them.
